The 3D cloak is implemented using a 15-element array of dipole antennas positioned 34 mm from the surface of a 753 mm tall, 101.5 mm radius conductive cylinder.
The cloak elements are arranged in 6 vertical columns with 125.6 mm spacing between element centers.
The experimental cloak configuration achieves a maximum scattering suppression of 34.2 dB, while the simulation-based configuration achieves 37.5 dB.
The experimental configuration shows better matching between the cloak and scattered fields, with an average suppression of 8.3 dB compared to 7.7 dB for the simulation-based weights.

Both the simulation and experimental configurations show similar functional bandwidths of around 13-14% and 3 dB bandwidths of 7.4% and 6.2% respectively when the cloak is configured for 1.2 GHz operation.
The experimental configuration maintains near-peak suppression over a wider frequency range but experiences a faster drop-off past 1.15 GHz.
The key challenges in implementing a multi-frequency active cloak include avoiding resonant mode scattering, mitigating element phase inversion, and addressing array aliasing at higher frequencies.

Future work includes improving the illumination and measurement capabilities to enable 3D verification of scattering suppression, integrating an incident field estimator to enable autonomous adaptation, and exploring additional cloak capabilities such as reconfigurability and multi-frequency operation.

Active cloaks can accommodate targets of virtually any size, shape, and material composition, as well as multiple frequencies and polarizations, unlike passive cloaks which have fundamental design and performance limitations.

The experimental setup uses a 1-18 GHz ridged horn antenna to illuminate the target, a 15-element array of 2.45 GHz whip dipole antennas as the cloak elements, and a network analyzer with a 16-channel controller to feed and weight the cloak elements.

This paper presents the first 3D implementation of an active electromagnetic interior cloak, expanding on previous 2D and quasi-2D designs to hide a conductive, cylindrical 3D target under free-space conditions.
The cloak is designed and validated through full-wave simulations and an experimental demonstration at 1.2 GHz.
The simulated cloak uses weights derived from the incident fields, while the experimental cloak uses weights determined by directly measuring the incident fields using a probe antenna.

The experimental configuration shows better matching between the cloak and scattered fields, likely due to accounting for apparatus-specific variances that are not present in the simulated environment.
The experimental cloak achieves peak performance at 1.18 GHz (8.6 dB suppression), while the simulated weights result in a peak frequency of 1.19 GHz (8.45 dB suppression).
